841.title: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
841.hook: sick and ready to give all his wealth away, he was told: a third is plenty (Bukhari)
841.howItsDone: In Islamic law a person may leave up to a third of their estate as a bequest, for charity or for people outside the fixed shares; the rest passes to heirs by the shares set in the Qur'an. Schools differ on the details.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Awf, who turned down half a fortune and asked for the market. Your line was rich and giving.

A man lies sick in Mecca, so sick he fears he will die there. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, comes to visit. And the sick man, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, has a plan ready. I have a lot of wealth, he says, and only one daughter to inherit from me. Shall I give two thirds of it away in charity? No. Half, then? No. A third? A third, the Prophet says, and a third is a lot. Today: a generous man stopped, kindly, from being too generous.
screen: `SICK IN MECCA.` → `TWO THIRDS? HALF?` → `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.`

segments.voice: Sa'd tells this himself, in Sahih al-Bukhari. He is ill and wants to do the most good he can with what he has left. The Prophet doesn't say: wonderful, give it all. He bargains him down, and then gives the reason, the heart of the day. It is better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them poor, holding out their hands to people. The daughter matters. Charity that leaves your own people begging has missed something. Then a second line, just as surprising: whatever you spend seeking God's pleasure, you are rewarded for it, even the bite of food you lift to your wife's mouth. So feeding your family is not the opposite of charity. It counts. Sa'd also feared dying in Mecca, the city he had left when he emigrated. The Prophet told him he might live on, so that some people would benefit through him and others be harmed. Tradition says he did live on. Muslim jurists use this visit as a foundation for the rule that a person may leave no more than a third of their estate as a bequest, with the rest passing to heirs by the shares the Qur'an sets. Different schools work out the details differently, but the third is traced back to this room. Generous enough to matter. Careful enough to leave no one behind.

segments.voice: Think of the places where you give: money, time, energy, attention. Look honestly for one where you give so much that the people closest to you go without, or one where you give nothing at all, and picture one small adjustment. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom in giving.
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. The companion who, sick in Mecca, wanted to give away most of his wealth, and was told a third is a lot, and that feeding his family counts too. Today's word.
Your line: a third is plenty. Feeding your own family counts too. Until tomorrow.

842.title: Abu Ubaydah
842.hook: called the trustworthy one of this community (Bukhari)
842.howItsDone: Muslims treat amanah, a trust, as a serious religious duty: deposits, promises, secrets and responsibilities are held as trusts, and Abu Ubaydah's title is one example teachers give.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, bargained down from two thirds to a third. Your line was a third is plenty.

Visitors from Najran come to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a request: send someone back with us, someone trustworthy. He answers: I will send you a man who is truly trustworthy, truly. In the room, people sit up. The report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the companions each hoped it would be them. Then he says: stand up, Abu Ubaydah. Today: the man the Prophet picked when the job was simply to be trusted.
screen: `SEND US SOMEONE TRUSTWORTHY.` → `EVERYONE HOPED.` → `STAND UP, ABU UBAYDAH.`

segments.voice: His full name was Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, and his story turns on one word. Bukhari records the Prophet saying: every community has its amin, its trustworthy one, and the amin of this community is Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah. To be amin is to be the person with whom things are safe: a deposit, a secret, a decision, a town far away that you're sent to serve. It's a strange kind of praise. Courage shows up on a battlefield; generosity shows up in a gift. Trustworthiness mostly shows up as nothing happening. The money is all there, the promise is kept, the secret stays secret, and nobody notices. Later, Bukhari places Abu Ubaydah among the commanders in Syria who rode out to meet the caliph Umar when plague broke out there. Umar decided to turn back. Abu Ubaydah asked him: are you running from God's decree? Umar answered: yes, we run from God's decree to God's decree. Trust doesn't mean always agreeing. It means you can say the hard thing to a friend and still be trusted. The man sent to Najran was the same man who would stand in Syria and put a hard question to the caliph.
screen: `EVERY COMMUNITY HAS ITS AMIN.` · `THE ONE WITH WHOM THINGS ARE SAFE.` · `TRUST LOOKS LIKE NOTHING HAPPENING.` · `GOD'S DECREE TO GOD'S DECREE.` · then, large: `TRUSTWORTHY OF THE UMMAH.`

segments.voice: Look at what's been handed to you lately: a friend's secret, a borrowed book, a small promise like I'll call you at six. Pick the one most likely to slip, and settle in your mind exactly how it will be kept, quietly, with no announcement. If you pray, you can ask to be someone with whom things are safe.

Your line: trustworthy of the ummah. Trust mostly looks like nothing happening. Rest well.

843.title: Khalid ibn al-Walid
843.hook: the commander whose horsemen turned Uhud against the Muslims, later fighting for them
843.howItsDone: Muslims teach that accepting Islam wipes out what came before it, and the companions' stories, Khalid's among them, are told as examples of former opponents welcomed and trusted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Ubaydah, the one the Prophet sent when a people asked for someone they could trust. Your line was trustworthy of the ummah.

Go back to the hillside at Uhud. The Muslims seem to be winning. The archers posted on a hill to guard the rear see the enemy running, leave their post, and come down for the spoils. The Qur'an, in the surah called the Family of Imran, speaks of that moment: some wanted this world, and the tide turned. Who turned it? The biographies name the man leading the Meccan horsemen, who saw the empty hill and rode around behind the Muslim lines: Khalid ibn al-Walid. Today: the man who broke the Muslims at Uhud, and what he did next.
screen: `THE ARCHERS LEAVE THE HILL.` → `HORSEMEN AROUND THE BACK.` → `KHALID IBN AL-WALID.`

segments.voice: Uhud cost the Muslims dearly. Companions we have met on this road died there, Mus'ab with his short cloak among them. Later, the biographies say, Khalid came to Medina to become Muslim. Picture that community the day he walked in: this is the man whose horsemen came around the hill. What does a community do with that? At Mu'tah, the battle where Ja'far and the other appointed leaders fell one after another, Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, telling the people in Medina what had happened. Zayd took the banner and fell. Ja'far took it and fell. Ibn Rawahah took it and fell. Then the banner was taken by one of the swords of God, and God gave them a way through. That sword was Khalid. Tradition calls him Saifullah, the sword of God. How does the man who broke the lines at Uhud become that? A report in Sahih Muslim gives the principle, through another Meccan who came over, Amr ibn al-As. When Amr hesitated, afraid of his past, the Prophet told him that Islam wipes out what came before it. The past is not erased from history; Uhud still happened. But it is not held against the man who turned. A community that believes people change can find its sword in its old enemy.

844.title: Abu Sufyan and Hind
844.hook: leaders of Mecca's opposition, who became Muslim when Mecca opened
844.howItsDone: Muslims remember the opening of Mecca as a day of amnesty, when former opponents, Abu Sufyan and Hind among them, were given safety and became Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khalid ibn al-Walid, who broke the lines at Uhud and later carried the banner. Your line was people change.

Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says it on the day Mecca opens, as Sahih Muslim records. A strange sentence, once you know whose house that was. At the end of Uhud, it was Abu Sufyan, leading the Meccan army, who called across the field: is Muhammad among the people? Is Abu Bakr? Is Umar? He cried out in praise of Hubal, the idol of Mecca, and the answer came back, as Sahih al-Bukhari records it: God is higher and more majestic. Now that same man's front door is named a refuge. Today: Abu Sufyan, and his wife Hind.
screen: `WHOEVER ENTERS HIS HOUSE IS SAFE.` → `IS MUHAMMAD AMONG THE PEOPLE?` → `GOD IS HIGHER.`

segments.voice: For years Abu Sufyan led Mecca's opposition to the Prophet. Hind, his wife, stood with him; the biographies tell hard stories of her at Uhud, around the death of the Prophet's uncle Hamzah. Then came the opening of Mecca, the conquest, when the Muslims entered the city and the enemy's house became a shelter. Abu Sufyan, the biographies say, became Muslim. Then Hind. Bukhari keeps her words, and they are startlingly honest. There was a time, she told the Prophet, when no household on the face of the earth was one I wanted humbled more than yours. Today, no household on the face of the earth is one I want honored more than yours. She didn't pretend the past away. She named it, then named the change. The Prophet answered with an oath of his own, by the One in whose hand is his soul. In the same report she goes straight on to a household problem: Abu Sufyan is tight with money; may she take what her children need? Yes, she's told, what is reasonable. From enemy of a house to ordinary questions within the community, in one conversation. They came late, after years of fighting, after Uhud and all it cost. Sunni tradition counts them among the companions. The door was not shut because they arrived at the end.
screen: `YEARS OF OPPOSITION.` · `THE ENEMY'S HOUSE, A SHELTER.` · `NO HOUSEHOLD I WANTED HUMBLED MORE.` · `NOW NONE I WANT HONORED MORE.` · then, large: `LATE, AND WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you once opposed, a rival, an old classmate, a relative you clashed with, and try Hind's two sentences quietly. Finish the first honestly, back then, I saw you as, and then the second, now, I see; if the second is hard to finish, that is worth knowing too. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

Your line: late, and welcome. Coming at the end still counts as coming. See you tomorrow.

845.title: Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl
845.hook: son of Abu Jahl, forgiven and welcomed, and his father not to be insulted in front of him (sirah)
845.howItsDone: Muslims are taught not to speak ill of the dead, and Ikrimah's story is told as an example of welcoming someone back without shaming them for their family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Sufyan and Hind, whose house became a place of safety when Mecca opened. Your line was late, and welcome.

Some names are hard to carry. Abu Jahl, father of ignorance, is the name tradition says the Muslims gave a leading enemy of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Mecca. The biographies say he fell at Badr, and that his son Ikrimah kept fighting after him. When Mecca opened and others were given safety, Ikrimah ran, south toward Yemen and the sea. A man with his father's name hanging over him, and every reason to think there is no way back. Today: what happened when he came back anyway.
screen: `A HARD NAME TO CARRY.` → `HE RAN FOR THE SEA.` → `HE CAME BACK ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: The biographies tell it this way. Ikrimah's wife, Umm Hakim, stayed in Mecca and became Muslim. She asked the Prophet for safety for her husband, and it was given. Then she went after him herself, all the way to the coast, and brought him home. One report adds a storm at sea, when the sailors told everyone aboard to call on God alone, and Ikrimah thought: if only God can save me at sea, only God can save me on land. A version of that scene is kept in Sunan an-Nasa'i, not in Bukhari. Before Ikrimah reached the city, the biographies say, the Prophet told his companions: Ikrimah is coming to you as a believer. Do not insult his father, because insulting the dead hurts the living and does not reach the dead. People had plenty of stories about Abu Jahl. The instruction was: not in front of his son. A report in Tirmidhi, from Ikrimah himself, gives the greeting he got: welcome to the rider, the emigrant. Not the son of the enemy. A traveler in from the road, greeted at the door. The same respect for the dead runs through a hadith in Bukhari, from Aisha: do not abuse the dead, for they have gone on to what they sent ahead.

846.title: Nusaybah bint Ka'b
846.hook: who fought at Uhud to shield the Prophet, and was praised by him
846.howItsDone: Muslims tell Nusaybah's story when they remember the women among the companions, and recite Surah al-Ahzab 33:35, which names believing men and women side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl, greeted as a rider come home. Your line was welcomed like a traveler.

Wherever I turned, to the left or to the right, I saw her fighting to defend me. The early historians put those words in the mouth of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about a day when the lines broke and men ran. The one he saw was a woman of Medina. In the old accounts, she had come to the field to give water to the thirsty and tend the wounded. When the danger reached him, she set the water down and fought. Her name was Nusaybah bint Ka'b, also called Umm Umarah. Today: the woman who stayed when others ran.
screen: `LEFT OR RIGHT, I SAW HER.` → `SHE CAME WITH WATER.` → `SHE SET IT DOWN AND FOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Nusaybah was one of the helpers of Medina; the biographies place her among those who pledged themselves to the Prophet before he ever came to their city. The day of the broken lines was Uhud. As the early historians tell it, she fought beside her husband and her sons to keep attackers away from him, and she was wounded. Then come his words: left or right, wherever he turned, she was there. Not that she was strong for a woman. That she was there, every time he looked. These accounts come from the sira and the early biographical works, not from Bukhari, so they are told as the historians tell them. A second scene, in Tirmidhi, is brave in a different way. Umm Umarah came to the Prophet and said: I see that everything is for men, and I don't see women mentioned at all. A direct question, to his face. Tirmidhi reports that in answer a verse came down, the thirty-fifth of the surah called the Clans. It runs through the believers pair by pair: men who surrender and women who surrender, men who believe and women who believe, the truthful, the patient, the humble, the charitable, the fasting, men and women each time, ending with forgiveness and a great reward prepared for them all. So Nusaybah stood her ground twice: once on a hillside, with a sword, and once in a room, with a question. The Qur'an itself, reports say, answered the second.

847.title: Asma bint Abi Bakr
847.hook: she of the two belts, who stood firm before a tyrant
847.howItsDone: Muslims tell Asma's story from Sahih al-Bukhari, where she cuts her belt for the journey to Medina, and Sahih Muslim, where she faces al-Hajjaj after her son's death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nusaybah, who stood her ground at Uhud. Your line was she stood her ground.

A bag of food, a skin of water, and nothing to tie them shut. Two men are about to slip out of Mecca in secret, and the provisions have to travel. The one packing them is the daughter of one of the two men. No cord, no strap, nothing. So she reaches for the cloth tied around her own waist. Decades later, a powerful man will try to use that moment to mock her son. It won't go the way he planned. Today: Asma, daughter of Abu Bakr.
screen: `FOOD, WATER, NOTHING TO TIE THEM.` → `SHE REACHES FOR HER OWN BELT.` → `DECADES LATER, A TAUNT.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari tells the first half. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr set out from Mecca for Medina, Asma prepared their food for the road. She could find nothing to tie the food bag and the water skin, so she cut her waistband in two, tied the food with one half and the water with the other, and from then on she was called she of the two belts. Sahih Muslim tells the second half, many years on. Her son, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, has been killed in Mecca by the forces of al-Hajjaj, the governor. Al-Hajjaj sends for his mother. She refuses. He sends again, with threats. She still refuses. So he goes to her and asks how she sees what he did to her son. She answers that he ruined her son's world, and her son ruined his hereafter. Then she picks up the insult he had been using. You call him the son of the woman of the two belts. Yes, I am she of the two belts. With one I tied up the food of the Messenger of God and of Abu Bakr. The other is the belt no woman does without. And she tells him a saying she heard from the Prophet, about a liar and a destroyer who would come from the tribe of Thaqif, and says plainly that she thinks the governor is the destroyer. The report says he got up and left without answering. Tradition remembers her as very old by then.

segments.voice: This week ran from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his third, through Abu Ubaydah, Khalid, Abu Sufyan and Hind, Ikrimah and Nusaybah, to Asma. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness in your later years.
